baghdad 🇮🇶 lecorbusier s most mysterious project the destiny of baghdad gymnasium is fascinating 1 it s almost a miracle that it actually exists 2 for many years its existence fell into obscurity in the architecture world 3 le corbusier s paternity remained controversial for quite some time in 1957 eight of the most important western architects le corbusier walter gropius josé luis sert gio ponti aalvar aalto and werner march constantine doxiadis were commissioned by king faisal ii to transform baghdad into a modern and cosmopolitan capital le corbusier was originally hired to create baghdad stadium and city of sport in support of the city s bid to host the 1960 olympics on july 14th 1958 just one day after the project was formally approved a coup d état ended the 37 year hashemite monarchy of iraq and the king was assassinated most of the large scale projects imagined by the starchitects were instantly abandoned as the iraqi capital didn t get the olympic games the construction of the complex was postponed le corbusier s passed away in 1965 thanks to the support of influential iraqi architect rifat chadirji a part of the sports city with reportedly little modification to the original plans would eventually be built under the supervision of french architect axel mesney between 1978 and 1980 and inaugurated under the name saddam hussein gymnasium for decades it suffered from the plight of being a posthumous work contested by the architecture purists it was never mentionned in the literature dedicated to the swiss born french architect it was perceived as a bastardized project not bearing the master s signature while researching for her thesis on modern architecture in baghdad in 2004 researcher caecilia pieri got interested in the complex after years of research in 2012 she managed to put a hand on never seen before construction archives at axel mesney s proving le corbusier s authorship the site was renovated a decade ago and is now fully functional it is mainly used for basketball and volleyball games facehunteriraq modernistarchitecture brutalist brutalistarchitecture concrete archi arch

baghdad 🇮🇶 burj abboud 1955 by rifatchadirji 1926 2020 and abdullah ihsan kamil 1919 1984 this bauhaus influenced tower represents the symbol of baghdad intense modernisation and westernisation in the 1950s it was back then the first high rise in town while the abboudbuilding includes some vernacular features such as archways screens and courtyards in response to the hot environment it remains mainly a project borrowing to the international style built at a time when chadirji was employed by the monarchy mandated under british rule it s really in the 1960s in a post monarchy republic that the father of iraqi modernism will fully express his unique style that he called international regionalism the idea was to combine ancient iraqi heritage with modern art and architecture to develop an iraqi aesthetic that was not only unique to iraq but also influence the development of a pan arab visual language with nearly 100 buildings chadirji contributed greatly to define the aesthetics of his country s public space especially through the 1970s by 1970 chadirji had offices throughout the middle east one of them was employing a young zahahadid in 1978 at the peak of his career he was wrongfully sentenced to life in prison but was eventually released after 20 months by saddam hussein who was seeking iraq s best architect to oversee the preparation of baghdad for an international conference in 1982 in 1983 chadirji eventually fled baghdad for teaching at harvard before relocating in the uk where he would spend the rest of his life the burj abboud survived miraculously six fires in 1985 1989 1996 1998 2005 2x it is nowadays partly unused brutalism brutalistarchitecture visitiraq travel travelphotography travelgram traveler travelling traveling instatravel travelawesome archi archidaily archilover archiporn arch archlovers archilovers baghdadarchitecture baghdad_iraq iraq_baghdad facehunteriraq

chinguetti 🇲🇷 has always been battling for its own survival against the sahara in the middle age it managed to become a major cultural intellectual religious and trading centre for many centuries the territory of most of present day mauritania was commonly known in the arab world as bilad shinqit the land of chinguetti 🌙 the city of libraries in is heyday it counted up to 30 libraries for a population of 20 000 people which housed thousands of arabic manuscripts the work of theologians writers jurists philosophers poets mathematicians and scientists ranging from the golden age of the almoravids in andalusia in the 11th century to the 20th century five libraries still remain and i got to visit one al habot 🌙 a center of science religion and mathematics mauritanians and other north western saharan islamic scholars have had a profound impact on islamic culture scholars bearing the title al shinqiti used to suggest strong scholarly expertise 🌙 a holy city the city was a principal gathering place for pilgrims of the maghreb on their way to mecca it eventually became known as a holy city in itself especially for pilgrims who couldn t make the long journey to the arabic peninsula 🌙 a massive trading center desert caravans transporting gold salt dates ivory and enslaved people across the sahara were the source of chinguetti s economic prosperity with as many as 30 000 camels gathering here at the same time historians believe that the spread of islam is intertwined with the development of the trans saharan trade as the religion established common values and a sense of trust among traders by the middle of the 19th century most trans saharan commercial arteries dried up replaced by maritime routes a desert is a place without expectation architecture mauritania 🇲🇷 riding the irontrain for 20 hours makes you feel slightly delirious 🌙 🌞💨 still trying to process the level of surrealism of sleeping dreaming and having tea on top of 22 000 tons of iron ore in motion in the middle of the sahara it is as well a special experience because this 704km long railway played an essentiel role in mauritania s history to exploit a humongous iron ore deposit in the deep desert a european conglomerate miferma created in the 1950s a city from scratch zouerat and built this railtrack to carry the raw mineral to the port of nouadhibou from where it is exported it provided the income for mauritania s economic development and rapid urbanisation during the first two decades of its independence 1960s 1970s in 1966 after only three years of operations iron mining contributed to 28 of the gdp and accounted for 92 of the value of all exports during the western sahara war in the 1970s the line became a target of the polisario front who partly destroyed it pushing eventually mauritania to drop its territorial claim on western sahara in 1979 the rail track nowadays briefly crosses the territory of the partially recognized state of the sahrawi arab democratic republic sadr the deserttrain plays as well the role of a lifeline for many people and remote desert communities who need to travel to visit family or search for work there is one passenger carriage at the very end of the world s longest 2 3km and heaviest train but most people ride it atop the iron ore big up to my partner in adventure ivonayw for joining me 🏻 train_nerds trainride trainrides trainadventures adventure adventuretime adventuretravel travel traveler traveling mauritanie facehuntermauritania

the curonianspit 🇱🇹 a miraculous 98km long sand dune peninsula connecting lithuania and russia before coming here i didn t know that such a place could exist depending if you are more into mythology or geology the sandspit was created by neringa a good hearted giantess to protect her coastline from an evil dragon or by the combined action of the sea wind and human activity over the last 5 000 years nevertheless the existence of this ephemeral territory is constantly under threat it would take very little to have it vanish completely after intensive logging in the 17th and 18th centuries the dunes began moving very fast and buried entire towns including nida nidden back then the main settlement from the 19th century onwards tree planting creation of a protective dune ridge along the seashore and limitation of public access have contributed to stabilise the spit nida is the last lithuanian town just 3km before the russian border there is something quite odd about the contrast between such a peaceful looking family friendly holiday destination dotted with 19th century wooden fisherman s houses and the tension of the war involving the big neighbour this coastal region has been the home of baltic and germanic cultures for many centuries with its incorporation in the german empire in the late 19th century nida became a summer hotspot for german artists and intellectuals have you been here or would you consider visiting kuršiųnerija куршскаякоса baltic baltics balticstate balticstates lietuva baltijosjūra facehunterlt
